stimulus.text: "It is... a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt.... It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone.... It is the cause of liberty." — Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged).
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Hamilton, defense of John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735; public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain primary source

books.section: E. The Development of Self-Government in Britain's New World Colonies

primary_sources: Hamilton, defense of John Peter Zenger (1735)

stem: What did the Zenger trial show about how press freedom advanced in the colonies?

options.text: That Parliament passed a law protecting truthful criticism of the government.
options.misconception: No act of Parliament protected truthful criticism; the acquittal came from a colonial jury, not from legislation.

options.text: That the royal governor issued a proclamation ending seditious-libel prosecutions.
options.misconception: The governor issued no such proclamation; he was the one who had Zenger prosecuted for criticizing him.

options.text: That a constitutional amendment guaranteed freedom of the press for printers.
options.misconception: No constitutional amendment existed in 1735; the Constitution and its Bill of Rights came decades later.

options.text: That a jury refused to convict, though the law stayed unchanged.

rationales.general:
1. Ask what actually changed in 1735. Background: a jury acquitted Zenger — and nothing else.
2. Ask what did not change. Background: no law was written, no statute repealed, no proclamation issued.
3. Ask what stayed on the books. Background: truth was still no defense against a charge of seditious libel.
4. Name the lesson. Press freedom advanced by a jury's refusal, not by a change in the law.
Remember: Zenger walked free because a jury said no — the law that had put him on trial stayed exactly where it was.
rationales.D: The Zenger trial changed no law: the judge barred Hamilton from arguing that truth was a defense, and truth stayed no defense against seditious libel on the books. What happened was a jury's refusal to convict — ordinary New Yorkers freeing a printer who had criticized the governor. Background: the acquittal became a landmark because it showed a jury could check royal power, not because it rewrote the law. Parliament passed nothing, the governor proclaimed nothing, and no constitution yet existed.
rationales.A: No act of Parliament protected truthful criticism; the acquittal came from a colonial jury, not from legislation.
rationales.B: The governor issued no such proclamation; he was the one who had Zenger prosecuted for criticizing him.
rationales.C: No constitutional amendment existed in 1735; the Constitution and its Bill of Rights came decades later.
